title: How carers can help with arthritis and frailty without taking over (UK)
meta_title: Helping Someone With Arthritis Without Taking Over
meta_description: Practical ways for family and carers to support someone with arthritis and frailty while protecting their independence, strength and confidence.
excerpt: Practical ways for family and carers to support someone with arthritis and frailty while protecting their independence, strength and confidence.
direct_answer: Carers help most by supporting, not replacing, what the person can still do. Doing tasks for someone can feel kind but may lead to weaker muscles and lost confidence. Agree what help is wanted, set up the task so they can do part of it, and get advice from an occupational therapist or physiotherapist.

content:
When someone you love has arthritis and is becoming frail, it is natural to want to do things for them. But doing everything can mean they lose strength, skills and confidence faster. The aim is to help in ways that keep them as able as possible.

This guide gives practical ideas for family members and carers. It is educational information, not personal medical advice.

Why doing everything can backfire

Muscles and skills weaken when they are not used. If a person stops dressing, making drinks or walking to the kitchen, those tasks can quickly become harder. Reablement services work on the same idea: helping people do things for themselves, rather than doing things for them.

Ask, do not assume

  • Ask what help is wanted, and when.
  • Agree which tasks they want to keep doing, even if slowly.
  • Respect their choices, even if you would do things differently.

Help with part of the task

  • Set things up so they can finish the task, for example getting clothes out so they can dress themselves.
  • Do the heavy or risky part, such as lifting a full kettle, and let them do the rest.
  • Allow extra time. Rushing increases the risk of falls.
  • Use equipment that makes tasks easier, such as long-handled aids, perching stools and jar openers.

Keep them moving

Encourage short, regular walks around the home, standing to do some tasks, and any exercises from a physiotherapist. Small amounts of activity spread through the day can help keep strength and balance.

Get professional advice

An occupational therapist can suggest equipment and safer ways of doing things. A physiotherapist can advise on exercise and walking aids. Ask the GP for a referral, or ask the council for a care needs assessment. As a carer, you can also ask for a carer's assessment of your own needs.

Look after yourself

Caring can be tiring and stressful. Carers UK and local carers centres offer advice and support, and respite care can give you a break.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

What if they are at risk of falling?

Talk to the GP about a falls assessment. Equipment, exercise and a medicines review can reduce risk, and a community alarm can bring help quickly.

What if they refuse help?

People have the right to make their own choices if they have capacity. Keep talking, offer options, and ask professionals for advice.

Am I entitled to support as a carer?

You can ask your council for a carer's assessment. You may also be eligible for Carer's Allowance, depending on your circumstances.
